name: The Joyce Theater
funding: Nonprofit foundation. Of $11.7M revenue in the year to August 2023, $5.5M was contributions and $5.4M program income (IRS Form 990); Philip Morris funded it from 1985.
watch: A 1990 Philip Morris report lists the Joyce in a presenters fund the company set up in 1985 (Philip Morris and the Arts, 1990).
why_flagged: Philip Morris's 1990 arts report lists the Joyce Theater among presenters supported by a fund the company created in 1985 (Philip Morris and the Arts: A 30-Year Celebration, 1990), and a Philip Morris file copy of a New York Times article of 26 September 1994 on the city's smoking bill names the Joyce (Truth Tobacco Industry Documents).

overview: The building opened as the Elgin Theater, a cinema, in 1941; it was gut-renovated in 1981-82 and reopened as the Joyce Theater with a gala on 2 June 1982 (Wikipedia).

Choreographer Eliot Feld and Cora Cahan, director of the Eliot Feld Ballet, conceived it as a theatre for smaller dance companies; it was named after the daughter of the philanthropist LuEsther Mertz (Wikipedia).
The theatre at 175 Eighth Avenue in Chelsea has 472 seats; in 2025 its auditorium was renamed for Anupam and Rajika Puri after a $15 million gift (Wikipedia).
The Joyce secured ownership of the building in 2015 and presents about 48 weeks of dance a year, with more than 340 performances for over 150,000 patrons (Joyce Theater Foundation, 2023 programme).
Linda Shelton, executive director since 1993, leads the Joyce Theater Foundation (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: The Joyce Theater: foundations and ticket income, with Philip Morris support from 1985
funding: The Joyce Theater Foundation reported total revenue of $11,655,562 for the year ending August 2023: contributions and grants $5,489,950, program service revenue $5,395,217 and investment income $642,788, against expenses of $13,367,597 and assets of $60,029,989 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
Revenue was $13,871,756 in the year ending August 2022, of which contributions and grants were $8,860,528 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).

The 2023 programme names the LuEsther T. Mertz Charitable Trust for leadership support, the Howard Gilman Foundation and The Shubert Foundation for annual programming, the Mellon Foundation for residencies, the Doris Duke Foundation for endowment funding and The Fan Fox & Leslie R. Samuels Foundation (Mark Morris Dance Group programme at the Joyce, August 2023).

The same programme thanks members of Congress for the federal Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program, which it says helped the theatre reopen (Mark Morris Dance Group programme at the Joyce, August 2023).

LuEsther Mertz underwrote the full cost of buying the building in 1979, and the conversion drew a $400,000 federal Urban Development Action Grant, a $450,000 National Endowment for the Arts challenge grant and Rockefeller Foundation money (Wikipedia).

Philip Morris created a fund in 1985 to support organizations that present innovative dance, performance art and theatre, and its 1990 report lists the Joyce Theater among them (Philip Morris and the Arts: A 30-Year Celebration, 1990).

red_flags.heading: Tobacco sponsorship
points: Philip Morris's 1990 report on its arts giving lists the Joyce Theater among presenting organizations supported by the fund it created in 1985 (Philip Morris and the Arts: A 30-Year Celebration, 1990).

A copy of Jonathan P. Hicks's New York Times article "Tobacco Industry Fights New York Over Smoking Bill", dated 26 September 1994 and filed in Philip Morris's records, names the Joyce Theater (Truth Tobacco Industry Documents, csj18d00).

wider_context: Philip Morris executives telephoned arts institutions that had benefited from the company's giving and asked them to put in a good word with Peter F. Vallone, the City Council Speaker, on the 1994 smoking bill; the source does not name the institutions (Tobacco Tactics, citing The New York Times, 5 October 1994).

A 1994 cartoon by R. J. Matson in The New York Observer showed Philip Morris using arts organizations it funded to lobby against the city's clean indoor air bill (Center for the Study of Tobacco and Society archive).
A February 2003 Joyce programme for David Gordon/Pick Up Company credits support from Altria Group, Inc. in the funding lines for the production (Joyce programme, 2003).

name: Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater
funding: Nonprofit foundation. Of $37.2M revenue in the year to June 2023, $19.1M was program income and $12.2M contributions (IRS Form 990); Bank of America sponsors its tours.
watch: Philip Morris was its principal corporate patron in the 1980s; a 1988 Ailey statement to a Surgeon General's committee meeting defended tobacco sponsorship (CSTS archive).
why_flagged: Philip Morris called itself a principal patron underwriting Ailey tours (Philip Morris and the Arts, 1990), announced a $500,000 grant in June 1990 (New York Times, 14 June 1990), and an Ailey statement of 27 October 1988 lauded it as principal benefactor (CSTS archive).

overview: Alvin Ailey founded the company in 1958 as Alvin Ailey and Company; Wikipedia describes it as the largest modern dance company in the United States (Wikipedia).
Judith Jamison led it as artistic director from 1989 to 2011 and Robert Battle from 2011 to 2023; Alicia Graf Mack took over on 1 July 2025 (Wikipedia).

Since 2005 the organization has been based at the Joan Weill Center for Dance, 405 West 55th Street, named after Joan Weill, who chaired the Alvin Ailey Dance Foundation for fourteen years (Wikipedia).
Joan and Sandy Weill co-chaired the building campaign, part of a five-year, $66 million capital campaign launched in 2000, and gave $18 million in total (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater: ticket income and donors, with Philip Morris as 1980s patron
funding: The Alvin Ailey Dance Foundation reported total revenue of $37,156,403 for the year ending June 2023: program service revenue $19,054,331, contributions and grants $12,208,696 and investment income $4,394,681, against expenses of $48,268,877 and assets of $257,305,406 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).

Revenue was $49,395,909 in the year ending June 2022, with contributions of $26,599,216, and $57,516,021 in the year ending June 2021, with contributions of $41,926,834 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).

Ailey's corporate funders as of 12 September 2025 were AARP, Akin Gump, American Express, Bank of America, Bloch, Bloomberg Philanthropies, BNY Mellon, Capital One, Deloitte, Diageo, Georgia-Pacific, Georgia Power, Goldman Sachs, The Home Depot Foundation, Prudential Foundation, TD Bank, Tito's Handmade Vodka, Warner Music Group/Blavatnik Fund and Wells Fargo (Ailey website).
Bank of America says it sponsors the company's 2026 and 2027 global tours (Bank of America website).
Sandy Weill gave a $16 million lead gift to the 2014 Campaign for Ailey's Future, and MacKenzie Scott gave $20 million in 2021 (Wikipedia).

Philip Morris wrote in 1990 that in the past decade it had been a principal patron of the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, underwriting tours of the United States, Latin America, Europe and Asia (Philip Morris and the Arts: A 30-Year Celebration, 1990).

At the opening of the new Ailey headquarters in June 1990, a $500,000 grant from Philip Morris was announced, with $25,000 more to help match a $300,000 Ford Foundation grant (The New York Times, Jennifer Dunning, 14 June 1990).

red_flags.heading: Tobacco sponsorship
points: A three-page statement by the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater for a meeting on tobacco sponsorship convened by the Surgeon General's Inter-Agency Committee on Smoking and Health, dated 27 October 1988, defends tobacco industry sponsorship of sports and the arts and lauds Philip Morris as the troupe's principal corporate benefactor (Center for the Study of Tobacco and Society archive).

A copy of Jonathan P. Hicks's New York Times article "Tobacco Industry Fights New York Over Smoking Bill", dated 26 September 1994 and filed in Philip Morris's records, names Alvin Ailey (Truth Tobacco Industry Documents, csj18d00).

wider_context: Philip Morris executives telephoned arts institutions that had benefited from the company's giving and asked them to put in a good word with Peter F. Vallone, the City Council Speaker, on the 1994 smoking bill; the source does not name the institutions (Tobacco Tactics, citing The New York Times, 5 October 1994).

A 1994 cartoon by R. J. Matson in The New York Observer showed Philip Morris using arts organizations it funded to lobby against the city's clean indoor air bill (Center for the Study of Tobacco and Society archive).

name: Perth Festival
funding: Not-for-profit company owned by UWA. Of $24.8M income in 2022-23, $7.7M was a Lotterywest grant and $1.6M corporate sponsorship (financial report); Chevron sponsored it until 2023.
watch: Chevron's 18-year sponsorship ended after the 2023 festival; the festival said the end was not linked to community backlash (ArtsHub, 18 October 2022).
why_flagged: Chevron sponsored the festival for 18 years until the 2023 festival (ArtsHub, 18 October 2022), after the Greens urged it on 1 March 2022 to drop fossil fuel sponsors (Australian Greens) and a campaign by Fossil Free Arts (Art Not Oil, 7 October 2022).

overview: Perth Festival describes itself as Australia's longest-running arts festival, founded by The University of Western Australia and held every summer for 70 years (Perth Festival website).
It is run by Perth International Arts Festival Limited, ABN 85 631 934 677, whose registered office is 3 Crawley Avenue, Crawley, and whose sole member is UWA (2022-23 financial report).
Ben Wyatt chairs the board; Marah Braye is chief executive and Anna Reece artistic director (Perth Festival website).
The 2025 festival drew 348,000 attendances, up from 215,000 in 2024, with more than 300 international and 620 Western Australian artists (2025 impact report).
details.funding_verdict: Perth Festival: Lotterywest and UWA grants, with Chevron as a sponsor until 2023
funding: Total revenue and income was $24,794,146 in 2022-23 ($17,125,305 in 2021-22): performance income $7,413,782, operating grants $8,310,000, fundraising and sponsorship $7,410,317, contra sponsorship $1,104,731 and other income $555,316 (2022-23 financial report).
Operating grants in 2022-23 were $7,700,000 from Lotterywest and $610,000 from The University of Western Australia; other government grants were $4,104,436 (2022-23 financial report).
Corporate sponsorship was $1,581,600 in 2022-23 and $1,747,393 in 2021-22; donations were $1,724,281 in 2022-23 (2022-23 financial report).
Lotterywest gave $9.6 million for the 2026 festival and has given the festival more than $177 million since 1991 (Lotterywest, 23 October 2025).

The partner page lists UWA as founding partner, Lotterywest as principal partner, City of Perth as city events partner and Wesfarmers Arts as Boorloo Contemporary partner, with Audio Technik, PAV, Tourism Western Australia and Western Power as premier partners (Perth Festival website).
Major partners listed are the Town of Cambridge, Clayton Utz, JCDecaux, My Place, The West Australian, Perth Now and Statewide Staging Systems (Perth Festival website).
Chevron's partnership with Perth Festival ran for 18 years and ended after the 2023 festival (ArtsHub, Jo Pickup, 18 October 2022).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuel sponsorship
points: The Australian Greens, through Senator Dorinda Cox and Dr Brad Pettitt MLC, urged Perth Festival on 1 March 2022 to end sponsorship deals with Woodside and Chevron, noting criticism from artists including Tim Winton, Stella Donnelly and Nick Allbrook (Australian Greens, 1 March 2022).

Fossil Free Arts, which said it had campaigned for over three years against the festivals' ties to Woodside and Chevron, welcomed the festival's announcement of 7 October 2022 that it would part with Chevron after the 2023 festival (Art Not Oil, 7 October 2022).
Executive director Nathan Bennett said Chevron's decision did not come as a surprise and was not linked to community backlash against Chevron (ArtsHub, 18 October 2022).

not_related: Woodside's sponsorship was of Fringe World and its organiser Artrage, a separate festival, which Woodside ended in 2023 (AAP, Liz Hobday).
wider_context: Fossil Free Arts welcomed the 2024 Fringe World and Perth Festival programs as Perth's first fossil free festival season, after a five-year campaign (AAP, Liz Hobday).

grade_basis: A funder tied to fossil fuels.

name: WA Museum Boola Bardip
funding: State statutory authority. Of $61.2M income in 2024-25, $49.0M came from the State Government; Woodside, Rio Tinto, BHP and Fortescue are partners (annual report).
watch: Woodside has funded WA Museum marine research since 1998, renewed for five years in August 2025, followed by a protest at its Maritime Museum.
why_flagged: The WA Museum extended Woodside's 28-year research partnership for five years on 6 August 2025 (WA Museum), people protested outside its Maritime Museum on 17 August 2025 (ArtsHub, 23 September 2025), and Crown was accommodation partner of its 2024-25 Terracotta Warriors exhibition (annual report).

overview: The Western Australian Museum was established in 1891 in the Old Perth Gaol; its Perth site closed on 18 June 2016 for redevelopment and reopened as WA Museum Boola Bardip on 21 November 2020 (Wikipedia).

The building in the Perth Cultural Centre was designed by OMA and Hassell and incorporates five heritage buildings, including the Old Perth Gaol of 1855, Hackett Hall and the Jubilee Building; the state pledged A$428 million for it in 2012 (Wikipedia).
Boola Bardip is Noongar for "many stories"; the museum network also runs the WA Maritime and WA Shipwrecks museums in Fremantle and museums in Albany, Geraldton and Kalgoorlie-Boulder (Wikipedia).
The museum recorded 1,647,208 visitors to museum and non-museum sites in 2024-25 (2024-25 annual report).
In December 2020 the museum removed two labels, on the origin of COVID-19 and on how Taiwan was shown on a map, after complaints including from the Chinese consul general in Perth (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: WA Museum Boola Bardip: state-funded, with oil, gas and mining partners
funding: Income from the State Government was $48.979 million in 2024-25, including $44.897 million service appropriation and $2.949 million state grants; other income was $12.220 million, including $4.798 million user charges and fees and $3.714 million other revenue (2024-25 annual report).

The annual report names BHP Group Ltd among sponsors, benefactors and granting agencies, and says a partnership with BHP enabled work on the taxonomy of terrestrial and freshwater invertebrates (2024-25 annual report).

The Foundation for the WA Museum lists Minderoo Foundation, Rio Tinto, the Stan Perron Charitable Foundation, Tianqi Lithium, Wesfarmers and Woodside Energy as founding partners, and Gold Fields, Fortescue, Northern Star Resources, Herbert Smith Freehills and Tattarang among major partners (2024-25 annual report).
The Woodside Energy: WA Down Under Gallery at the WA Maritime Museum reopened in December 2024 after 12 months of refurbishment (2024-25 annual report).

Woodside has supported the museum's marine biodiversity research since 1998, and on 6 August 2025 the collaboration was extended for five years for research along the Gascoyne coast; no figure was published (WA Museum, 6 August 2025).

Corporate partners of the Terracotta Warriors: Legacy of the First Emperor exhibition included Cathay Pacific as airline partner, Crown as accommodation partner and Norton Gold Fields (2024-25 annual report).
Crown Perth is a resort and casino in Burswood owned by Crown Resorts (Wikipedia).

Fortescue entered a three-year research partnership on biodiversity in the Fortescue Marsh, and Gold Fields a three-year partnership as presenting partner of two regional museum projects (2024-25 annual report).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuel partnership
points: The WA Greens and the Conservation Council of WA condemned the renewed Woodside partnership during a marine heatwave that killed coral along about 1,500 km of coast; Woodside sponsored free entry to the WA Maritime Museum on 17 August 2025 (The Guardian, 13 August 2025, via Glass Wings).

The museum stated on 17 August 2025 that Woodside neither directs nor participates in the research, which has found no less than 700 new species, and that the museum keeps the intellectual property (WA Museum, 17 August 2025).

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: A protest took place outside the WA Maritime Museum on its Woodside-sponsored family open day on 17 August 2025 (ArtsHub, Jo Pickup, 23 September 2025).
VOICES for Climate sang outside the Australian Energy Producers' annual conference event at WA Museum Boola Bardip on a Monday evening in May 2024 (Perth Voice, 23 May 2024).

grade_basis: Funders tied to fossil fuels and gambling. The record also holds a public protest.
